title: Yorkshire Pudding
subtitle: Classic British batter pudding, risen and crisp
excerpt: The iconic British batter pudding: milk, eggs, and flour poured into smoking-hot fat and baked until puffed, golden, and hollow inside. Essential with a British roast.

recipe.sourceNotes: Yorkshire pudding has been made in northern England since at least the eighteenth century. The earliest recipe in print appears in 1737 in Hannah Glasse's The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy under the name 'dripping pudding', describing a batter cooked under a roasting spit to catch the drippings. Yorkshire pudding as made today is cooked in small individual tins or a large shallow tin. The traditional use was as a first course before the meat at Sunday lunch: it was originally served with gravy to fill the stomach before the meat, which was more expensive. Today it is served alongside the roast. The Yorkshirewoman's unofficial commandment holds that the fat must be smoking hot, the batter must rest, and the oven door must not be opened during baking. Breaking any of these rules reliably prevents the pudding from rising.

recipeTools.notes: A 12-hole deep muffin tin, or a shallow 30 x 20 cm roasting tin for one large pudding.

content.text: Three non-negotiable rules: the batter must rest for at least 30 minutes; the fat must be smoking hot before the batter goes in; the oven door must not be opened during baking. Breaking any of these will result in flat, rubbery puddings. The batter should be the consistency of double cream. Use equal parts egg and milk by volume, and half that volume of flour.

Whisk together the flour, eggs, milk, and salt in a jug until completely smooth. The batter should be the consistency of double cream. Rest for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to several hours in the fridge.
Heat the oven to 230 C / fan 210 C / gas 8. Add a little oil to each hole of a 12-hole muffin tin. Heat in the oven for 10 to 15 minutes until the fat is smoking hot.

Working quickly, pour the batter into the hot tin, filling each hole about a third full. The batter should sizzle on contact. Return to the oven immediately. Do not open the oven for 20 minutes. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until well risen and deeply golden. Serve immediately.
